title: Detective Challenge
goal: I can solve mixed word problems and money problems on my own.

card.desc: Bristol proves she can solve mixed word problems at the Pathways Week 7 level: price × how many, skip counting money, finding how many she can buy, comparing costs, and the words price, total, factor, product and multiple. After she passes, she retakes Pathways Week 7 Math with Jonathan and needs 85.

win: Case closed! You are ready for the Trading Post!

slides.title: Detective Challenge: On Your Own
slides.text: You proved it in class. Now solve the cases on your own! 🕵️

slides.title: Detective checklist

steps.text: ✖️ Same price or equal groups → multiply. ➕ Different things → add. ➖ Spend or compare → subtract.
✅ Check: too big or too small? After you subtract, add back.

slides.tip: How many can I buy? Count the jumps, not the last number.

slides.title: Say it out loud
slides.text: Say these out loud. You can tell your mom!

items.q: Scarves cost $7 each. Ellie buys 5. What is the total?
items.no: Every scarf is $7. Multiply. Then check your math.

items.q: Liz has $40. She buys a toy for $23. How much is left?
items.why: She spends money, so subtract. 40 − 23 = 17. Check: 17 + 23 = 40.
items.no: She spends money. Subtract. Then check your math.
items.hint: Regroup a ten. Then add back to check.

items.q: A puppy bed is $19. A blanket is $15. Amy buys both. What does she pay?
items.no: She buys both. Different things → add. Then check your math.

items.q: Hats cost $10 each. Marion has $50. How many hats can she buy?
items.no: Skip count by 10s until you reach 50. Count the jumps.

items.q: Bows cost $4 each. Ellie pays $36. How many bows did she buy?
items.no: Skip count by 4s until you reach 36. Count the jumps.

slides.title: Which operation?
slides.text: Read the whole story. Tap it. Then tap the right box.

items.text: Liz earned $7 walking dogs and $8 washing cars. How much did she earn?
items.why: $7 and $8 are different amounts. They join. 7 + 8.
items.hint: Is it the same amount each time?

items.text: There are 4 tables. Each table has 9 cups.
A leash is $15. A collar is $8. How much less is the collar?
Amy had $25. She bought a book for $9.
items.why: She paid money. It goes away. 25 − 9.
items.hint: Did Amy get money or pay money?

items.text: Marion buys 3 bags of food for $8 each.
items.hint: Does every bag cost the same?

items.text: Ellie has 16 stickers. Her mom gives her 7 more.
items.hint: Are stickers joining or going away?

slides.done: Case closed! You read every story carefully.

items.q:
Amy says: 7 packs at $6 each is $13.
What is the right total?
items.why: Amy added. Same price for each pack, so multiply. 7 × 6 = 42.
items.no: Every pack is $6. Multiply, do not add. Then check your math.

items.q:
Liz says: A bed is $20. A mat is $12. The bed is $32 more.
How much more is the bed really?
items.why: Liz added. How much more means compare. 20 − 12 = 8.
items.no: How much more means subtract. Then check your math.

items.q: Skip count by 10s: 10, 20, 30. These numbers are ____ of 10.
items.why: Numbers you land on when you skip count are multiples.
items.no: What do we call the numbers you land on when you skip count?
items.hint: It starts with m: m _ l t i p l e s

items.q: Bows are $6 each. Liz buys 5. She pays $30. Which number is the total?
items.why: The total is what she pays for all of them: $30.
no: $6 is the price of one bow.
5 is how many bows she buys.

items.hint: Count by 4s: 4, 8, 12 … until you reach 32. How many jumps?

items.why: 9 × 7 = 63. Check: 10 sevens is 70. Take away one 7: 63. ✔
items.hint: 10 sevens is 70. Take away one 7: 63. How many sevens is that?

sets.q: Birdhouses cost $10 each. The club buys 9. What is the total?
sets.no: Every birdhouse is $10. Multiply. Then check your math.

sets.q: Collars cost $9 each. Liz buys 4. What is the total?
sets.no: Every collar is $9. Multiply. Then check your math.

sets.q: Marion has $45. Bird toys cost $5 each. How many can she buy?
sets.no: Skip count by 5s until you reach 45. Count the jumps.

sets.q: A bed costs $42. A blanket costs $18. How much more is the bed?
sets.no: How much more means subtract. Then add back to check.

sets.q: Ellie buys a leash for $16 and a bowl for $9. What does she pay?
sets.no: Two different things. Add. Then check your math.

sets.q: Amy buys 3 toys at $8 each. Liz buys 5 toys at $5 each. Who spends more?
no: Amy spends 3 × 8 = $24. Find Liz's total: 5 × 5.
Find both totals. Are $24 and $25 the same?

sets.q: Bones are $4 each. Ellie pays $28 for 7 bones. What is the $28?
sets.why: $28 is what she pays for all 7 bones. That is the total.
no: The price is for one bone: $4.
7 is the number of bones.

sets.q: Liz says: 6 bags of treats at $9 each is $15. What is right?
sets.why: Same price for each bag, so multiply. 6 × 9 = 54.
no: Liz added 6 + 9. Every bag is $9, so multiply.
$63 is 7 × 9. There are 6 bags.

sets.q: Bird feeders cost $10 each. Amy buys 6. What is the total?
sets.no: Every feeder is $10. Multiply. Then check your math.

sets.q: Bags of hay cost $8 each. The club buys 7. What is the total?
sets.no: Every bag is $8. Multiply. Then check your math.

sets.q: Ellie has $70. Collars cost $10 each. How many collars can she buy?
sets.no: Skip count by 10s until you reach 70. Count the jumps.

sets.q: A fish tank is $53. A lamp is $27. How much more is the tank?
sets.no: How much more means subtract. Then add back to check.

sets.q: Liz buys a cage for $38 and a mat for $15. What does she pay?
sets.no: Two different things. Add. Then check your math.

sets.q: Marion buys 4 bags at $7 each. Ellie buys 3 bags at $9 each. Who spends more?
no: Ellie spends 3 × 9 = $27. Find Marion's total: 4 × 7.
Find both totals. Are $28 and $27 the same?

sets.q: Treats are $6 a bag. Amy buys 5 bags for $30. What is the $6?
sets.why: $6 is what one bag costs. That is the price.
no: The total is for all 5 bags: $30.
5 is the number of bags.

sets.q: Ellie says: 9 brushes at $4 each is $13. What is right?
sets.why: Same price for each brush, so multiply. 9 × 4 = 36.
no: Ellie added 9 + 4. Every brush is $4, so multiply.
$32 is 8 × 4. There are 9 brushes.

sets.q: Dog coats cost $10 each. The shelter buys 8. What is the total?
sets.no: Every coat is $10. Multiply. Then check your math.

sets.q: Fish bowls cost $6 each. Liz buys 8. What is the total?
sets.no: Every bowl is $6. Multiply. Then check your math.

sets.q: Amy has $50. Rubber ducks cost $5 each. How many ducks can she buy?
sets.no: Skip count by 5s until you reach 50. Count the jumps.

sets.q: A scooter is $61. A helmet is $29. How much more is the scooter?
sets.no: How much more means subtract. Then add back to check.

sets.q: Marion buys a bed for $27 and a bowl for $18. What does she pay?
sets.no: Two different things. Add. Then check your math.

sets.q: Liz buys 2 toys at $9 each. Amy buys 3 toys at $6 each. Who spends more?
sets.why: Liz: 2 × 9 = 18. Amy: 3 × 6 = 18. They spend the same.
no: Liz spends 2 × 9 = $18. Find Amy's total: 3 × 6.
Amy spends 3 × 6 = $18. Find Liz's total: 2 × 9.

sets.q: Hats are $7 each. Ellie buys 6 hats. She pays $42. What is the $42?
sets.why: $42 is what she pays for all 6 hats. That is the total.
no: The price is for one hat: $7.
6 is the number of hats.

sets.q: Marion says: 8 bowls at $5 each is $13. What is right?
sets.why: Same price for each bowl, so multiply. 8 × 5 = 40.
no: Marion added 8 + 5. Every bowl is $5, so multiply.
$35 is 7 × 5. There are 8 bowls.

practice.intro: Three tries on each one. Only your first try counts. Use your detective checklist on every story.

questions.q: Tickets to the pet show cost $10 each. The family buys 5. What is the total?
questions.no: Each ticket is $10, so multiply. Then check your math.

questions.q: Kitten toys cost $5 each. Ellie has $30. How many can she buy?
questions.no: Skip count by 5s until you reach 30. Count the jumps.

questions.q: Bird cages cost $9 each. The shop sells 6. What is the total?
questions.no: Each cage is $9, so multiply. Then check your math.

questions.q: Amy had $34. She spent $19. How much is left?
questions.why: She spent money, so subtract. 34 − 19 = 15. Check: 15 + 19 = 34.
questions.no: She spent money. Subtract. Then check your math.
questions.hint: Regroup a ten: 14 − 9 in the ones.

questions.q: A cat bed is $23. A cat tree is $38. Liz buys both. What does she pay?
questions.no: She buys both, so add. Then check your math.

questions.q: Which of these stories is a multiply story?
choices: Marion pays $7 for a ball and $4 for a bone.
There are 8 rabbits. Each one eats 3 carrots.
A rope is $12. A ball is $5. How much more is the rope?
no: Two different prices. That is add.
How much more means compare. That is subtract.

questions.q: Collars are $7 each. Amy buys 7. What is the total?
no: $14 is 7 + 7. That is only 2 collars.
$42 is 6 × 7. Amy buys 7 collars.

questions.why: Skip count by 5s and you land on 15, 25 and 35.
no: 12 is not a multiple of 5.
14 is not a multiple of 5.

questions.q: Treats cost $4 a bag. Liz pays $24. How many bags did she buy?
questions.no: Skip count by 4s until you reach 24. Count the jumps.

questions.q:
Ellie says: 5 brushes at $8 each is $13.
What is the right total?
questions.no: Ellie added. Same price for each brush means multiply. Then check your math.

questions.q: Amy buys 4 bags at $6 each. Marion buys 3 bags at $9 each. Who spends more?
no: Amy spends 4 × 6 = $24. Find Marion's total: 3 × 9.
Find both totals. Are $24 and $27 the same?

questions.q: Leashes are $10 each. Ellie buys 3. She pays $30. Which numbers are the factors?
questions.why: You multiply the price by how many: 10 × 3 = 30. The factors are 10 and 3.
no: 30 is the product, the total she pays.
30 is the product. Which two numbers do you multiply?

teacher.objective: Bristol solves mixed one-step word problems on her own at the Pathways Week 7 level: price × how many, skip counting $5 and $10, how many she can buy (missing factor), comparing costs, adding two prices, spending, and the words price, total, factor, product and multiple. Week 4 Day 3 (Prove it). Passing this check means she is ready to retake Pathways Week 7 Math with you.
materials: Play money ($5 and $10 bills, plus about 24 $1 bills) and the price-tag cards from Tuesday
Index card for her detective checklist
Her book, Amy and the Missing Puppy
Printed packet (2 pages) to send home
The Class lesson open on your laptop (course page, code 9110)
A laptop or tablet for the Pathways Week 7 Math retake
Paper and pencil for the Pathways "Step Away From the Screen" step, plus the Week 7 Math Pre/Post sheet (Pre/Post link on the Pathways Grade 3 course page) if you use it

plan.do: Class slide 1. She says the 3 detective questions from memory.
Class slide 2. She retells the story so far with first, next, then, and predicts the ending with a clue.
Class slide 3. Check Tuesday's After-Class score and Wednesday's work first. She names the strategy before each answer.
Class slides 4–5. She copies the checklist onto an index card and uses it on each warm-up case. On $50 − $27: too big or too small?
Class slide 6. Six tricky stories; she names the operation with no hints.
Class slides 7–9. She buys toy mice with $5 bills one at a time, builds $24 into $4 piles, then solves two on her own.
Class slides 10–11. You make a regrouping mistake on purpose and she catches it by adding back; then she names each student's mistake before choosing.
Class slides 12–13. She says and spells price, total, factor, product, multiple; names multiples of 5 and 10; answers the word questions.
Class slide 14. Numbers only for money, first try counts, read aloud, check spelling.
Class slide 15. Show the task list (split by week). If time allows, she starts the After-Class Lesson right away while you are there (see notes).

watch: Adding the price and the number of items (9 + 5 for 9 bags at $5). Ask: does every bag cost the same?
Giving the last skip-count number instead of the number of jumps on "how many can she buy". Have her lay down one bill per toy.
Regrouping slips in money subtraction ($50 − $27 as $33, $42 − $18 as $36). Ask her to check by adding back.
"In all" read as multiply when the amounts are different ($9 and $8 spent on two days).
Mixing up price and total. The price is for one; the total is for all.
Spelling the five words when she says them: price, total, factor, product, multiple. In Pathways she must type them correctly.
In the Pathways retake: typing $ in a money answer (marked wrong and costs the first-try points). Remind her before she starts: numbers only.

packet_key.answer: price → what one thing costs; total → the whole amount you pay; factor → a number you multiply; product → the answer when you multiply; multiple → a number you land on when you skip count
Any prediction with a reason, in a complete sentence with a capital letter and a period.

teacher.notes: Pathways Week 7 Math retake (needs 85): start it only after she scores 85 or more on today's Show What You Know (the end of the After-Class Lesson). Best plan: she does the After-Class Lesson right after class while you are there (about 25 minutes); if she passes, do the retake right after (about 30 minutes). Otherwise do it at the start of Lesson 12 (the task list tells Tia it is done with you, not alone). Sit beside her and let her work; she types her first and last name on the first screen, reads each question aloud, and uses the detective checklist. Do not give answers. How it scores: 2 tries per question, but only a first-try right answer earns points, and the score is out of 100 (85 to master). Typed answers must match exactly: money totals as a plain number (30, not $30); the multiplication-sentence item wants a small x with spaces (3 x 4, not 3x4); and price, total, factor and multiple are typed in Type-It and the Boss Battle, so she checks spelling before pressing Check. Every Pathways pricing item uses $5 or $10 prices only. The "Step Away From the Screen" slide asks about her paper work, so have paper and pencil ready. The video, the contractions bonus, Bonus Practice and the Speed Arena do not count toward her score. Week 7 Math opens only when Week 6 Math is mastered on that same device; on a different laptop or tablet it shows a lock, so she types 1111 (or you type 9110). If she scores under 85 on Pathways, it gives a fresh question set on the next attempt (3 sets that rotate): review the misses with class slides 7–9 (how many can I buy) and 12–13 (math words) of this lesson and the Practice set, then retry on another day. If she scores under 85 on today's Show What You Know, do not start the retake: redo the play-money shop and the Practice set, then she retakes Show What You Know (a new question set) first. The break task list runs week by week up to Lesson 12; it includes page 2 of the Lesson 10 Packet and Times Table Trail, Lesson 7.

tasks: Thursday, right after class: do the After-Class Lesson. Pass Show What You Know with 85.
Thursday, after you pass: do Pathways Week 7 Math again with Jonathan (link above, under Also do). You need 85. Not done yet? Do it with Jonathan at the next lesson.
Break week 1: do the Lesson 11 Practice.
Break week 1: do page 2 of the Lesson 10 Packet.
Break week 2: do the Lesson 11 Packet, pages 1 and 2.
Break week 3: do Times Table Trail, Lesson 7 (link above, under Also do).
Every break week: read your book for 15 minutes a day, 4 days a week.

slides.title: Detective Challenge
slides.text: Today you prove it. You solve tricky stories all by yourself! 🕵️

notes.do: Set out the play money ($1, $5, $10 bills), the price-tag cards from Tuesday, 3–4 toys and the whiteboard.
notes.say: "This week you learned to be a word problem detective. Today you PROVE it. I will help less and less as we go."
notes.listen: All three from memory. If she stalls, give the first word of each (What … Are … Which …).

slides.title: The story so far
slides.text: Think about Amy and the Missing Puppy.
prompts: Tell me the story so far. What happened first, next and then?
Who helps look for the puppy?
How do you think the story will end? What clue makes you think so?
starters: I think it will end … because …

notes.do: Book talk, about 6 minutes. Retelling in order is her strength; let her lead.
notes.ask: "First, next, then?" "Who helps?" "How will it end? What clue makes you think so?"
notes.listen: Signal words in order (first, next, then) and a prediction tied to a clue. If she gives a prediction without a clue, ask: "What part of the book made you think that?"

items.q:
7 × 8 = ?
Hint: double the 4s fact.
no: 54 is 6 × 9. It is a common mix-up with 7 × 8!
63 is 7 × 9. Find 7 × 4, then double it.
32 is 36 − 4. You need the number that times 4 makes 36.

items.q: Brushes cost $6 each. Ellie buys 7. What is the total?
no: $13 is 6 + 7. Every brush costs $6, so multiply.
$48 is 8 × 6. She buys 7 brushes.

notes.do: Check Tuesday's After-Class score and Wednesday's work first. She names the strategy before answering.
notes.ask: "7 × 8: double which fact?" "4 × ? = 36: what times 4 makes 36?" "7 brushes at $6: how do you find 7 × 6?"
notes.listen: 56 (double 28), 9 (double 9 is 18, double 18 is 36), $42 (35 + 7). If she says 54 for 7 × 8, have her say "5, 6, 7, 8: 56 = 7 × 8."

slides.title: Detective checklist

steps.text: 🔍 What is happening? Say it in your own words.
✅ Check. Is the answer too big or too small?

slides.tip: The total for many things at the same price is bigger than the price. If your total is small, look again!

notes.do: She reads the checklist aloud once. Copy it onto an index card she keeps next to her for the rest of the lesson.
notes.say: "Today you use this checklist on every story. The last step is new: check if your answer makes sense."
notes.ask: "If 8 collars cost $7 each, could the total be $15? Too big or too small?"
notes.listen: "Too small. 8 collars cost more than that."

items.q: The club sells 9 dog scarves. Each one is $4. How much money does the club get?
items.why: Same price for each scarf. 9 × 4: double 9 is 18, double 18 is 36.
no: $13 is 9 + 4. Each scarf is $4, so multiply.
$32 is 8 × 4. The club sells 9 scarves.

items.q: Amy has $50. She buys a bed for $27. How much money is left?
items.why: She spends money, so subtract. 50 − 27 = 23. Check: 23 + 27 = 50.
no: $77 is 50 + 27. She spends money, so subtract.
Check: 33 + 27 = 60, not 50. Regroup a ten and try again.

items.q: Ellie buys 8 packs of cards at $6 each. Which number sentence finds the total?
items.why: Same price for every pack. 8 × 6 = 48 (4 × 6 = 24, double it).
no: Every pack costs $6. That is equal groups, so multiply.
8 × 6 is not 42. 7 × 6 = 42. Double 4 × 6 instead.

notes.do: She solves each case on the whiteboard first, then answers. Point to the checklist card on each one.
notes.ask: On $50 − $27: "Too big or too small? How can you check?"
notes.listen: $36, $23 (check: 23 + 27 = 50), 8 × 6 = 48. On the last item she must reject 8 × 6 = 42: the operation is right but the fact is wrong.

slides.title: Which operation?
slides.text: These are tricky! Read the whole story. Then name the operation.

items.q:
Marion spent $9 on Monday and $8 on Tuesday. How much did she spend in all?
Add, subtract or multiply?
items.why: Different amounts on two days, so add. 9 + 8 = 17.
items.no: Is it the same amount each day?

items.q:
There are 5 shelves. Each shelf holds 7 cans. How many cans in all?
Add, subtract or multiply?

A hat costs $14. A scarf costs $9. How much less is the scarf?
Add, subtract or multiply?
items.no: Less asks you to compare two prices.

items.q:
Ellie had $30. She paid $8 for a book. How much does she have now?
Add, subtract or multiply?
items.why: She paid money, so it goes away. 30 − 8.
items.no: Did Ellie get money or pay money?

items.q:
Liz bought 6 stickers for $2 each.
Add, subtract or multiply?
items.no: Does every sticker cost the same?

items.q:
Amy saved $12. Then her mom gave her $5.
Add, subtract or multiply?
items.no: Is money joining or going away?

notes.do: She reads each story aloud, names the operation without help, then types it on your laptop herself. Do not hint until she has answered.
notes.ask: Only if she is wrong: "What is happening? Is it the same amount each time?"
notes.listen: The trap is Marion's $9 and $8 "in all": different amounts, so add (not multiply). How much less is compare, so subtract.

slides.title: How many can I buy?
slides.text: Liz has $35. Toy mice cost $5 each. How many can she buy?

steps.text: Skip count by 5 until you reach 35.

slides.tip: The answer is the number of jumps, not the last number you say.

notes.do: Reveal step by step. Hand her $35 in $5 bills. She "buys" toy mice one bill at a time and lines up a toy (or index card) for each bill.
notes.say: "Now the question changes. We know the money. We find how many things we can buy."
notes.ask: "How many bills did you use? How many mice did you get? Are those the same number?"
notes.listen: 7 bills, 7 mice. The answer is the number of jumps, not 35.

slides.title: How many bows?
slides.text: Bows cost $4 each. Liz has $24. Make one group of $4 for each bow. Use all $24.
slides.why: 6 groups of $4 make $24. Liz can buy 6 bows. 6 × 4 = 24.
slides.hint: Each group is $4. Keep making groups until you reach $24. Count the groups.

notes.do: Give her 24 $1 bills. She makes piles of $4 until the money is gone, then sets the counters on screen.
notes.ask: "How many piles? What does each pile buy? So how many bows?" Then write ? × 4 = 24 and ask what the missing factor is.
notes.listen: 6 piles, 6 bows, the missing factor is 6. If she answers 24, ask: "Is 24 bows or dollars?"

items.q: Leashes cost $10 each. Ellie has $60. How many leashes can she buy?
no: $60 is her money. Count the jumps of 10.
7 leashes would cost $70. Count the jumps again.

items.q: Bones cost $4 each. Marion pays $32. How many bones did she buy?
no: 28 is 32 − 4. The question asks how many bones.
9 bones would cost 4 × 9 = $36.

notes.do: Guided practice. She uses play money on the first one, then tries the second with skip counting only.
notes.listen: 6 leashes; 8 bones. If she says 28 on the second, she subtracted 4: ask "How many bones?"

slides.title: Does my answer make sense?
slides.text: Detectives check their answers. Ask: too big or too small?

steps.text: 9 bags at $5 each. Is $14 right? 🤔 No! 3 bags already cost $15. 9 bags cost much more. 9 × 5 = $45.
A cage is $43. A mat is $18. How much more is the cage? I got $35. Check: 35 + 18 = 53. Not 43! ❌

slides.tip: Many things at the same price → the total is much bigger than the price. After you subtract, add back to check.

notes.do: Model the thinking out loud on the whiteboard. On the second step, make the regrouping mistake on purpose (43 − 18: you write 35 because you did 8 − 3) and let her catch it with the add-back check.
notes.say: "I made a mistake on purpose. Can you find it?"
notes.ask: "Is $14 too big or too small for 9 bags? Why?" "How do we check a subtraction?"
notes.listen: "Too small: 3 bags already cost $15, so 9 bags cost way more." "Add back: 25 + 18 should make 43."

items.q: Liz says: 9 bags at $5 each. 9 + 5 = $14. What is the right total?
items.why: Same price for 9 bags, so multiply. 9 × 5 = 45.
no: Liz added. Every bag costs $5, so multiply.
$40 is 8 × 5. There are 9 bags.

items.q: Amy says: A cage is $16. A bed is $9. The cage costs $25 more. What is right?
no: $25 is 16 + 9. More here means compare, so subtract.
$9 is the price of the bed, not the difference.

items.q: Ellie says: 8 collars at $7 each is $54. What is right?
no: 54 is 6 × 9. Check 8 × 7 with double the 4s.
$15 is 8 + 7. Every collar is $7, so multiply.

notes.do: She is the teacher. For each one she says what the student did wrong BEFORE she picks the right answer.
notes.ask: "What did Liz do? What did Amy do? What did Ellie do?"
notes.listen: Liz added instead of multiplying; Amy added instead of comparing; Ellie used the right operation but the wrong fact (54 is 6 × 9).

slides.title: Get ready for the Trading Post
slides.text: Soon you take Pathways Week 7 Math again with Jonathan. You will type some answers. Let's practice the words.
prompts: Say and spell each word out loud: price, total, factor, product, multiple.
Use price and total in one sentence about a pet shop.
starters: The price is … so the total is …

notes.do: She says and spells each word out loud. You write what she spells exactly as she says it, then she checks your writing against the slide.
notes.say: "In Pathways you will type these words, and only your first try counts. Let's get the spelling right now."
notes.listen: price, total, factor, product, multiple, all spelled right. Multiples: any skip-count landing spots (10, 20, 30; 5, 10, 15).

items.q: Hats are $5 each. Amy buys 4. She pays $20. Which number is the price?
items.why: The price is what one hat costs: $5.
no: 4 is how many hats she buys.
$20 is the total, what she pays for all of them.

items.q: Which list shows only multiples of 10?
items.why: Skip count by 10s: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60. You land on 20, 40 and 60.
no: 15 is a multiple of 5, but not of 10.
5 and 15 are multiples of 5, not of 10.

items.q: In 9 × 4 = 36, what is 36 called?
items.why: The answer when you multiply is the product.
no: The factors are 9 and 4. They are the numbers you multiply.
Price is what one thing costs. This is a fact, not a price tag.

notes.do: Quick check for understanding. She answers and explains each one.
notes.ask: "Why is $20 not the price?" "Why is 15 not a multiple of 10?" "What are the factors in 9 × 4 = 36?"
notes.listen: Price is for one hat; 15 is not a 10s landing spot; factors 9 and 4, product 36.
